cards.statement: A subnet's primary IPv4 range can expand after creation when the new range avoids conflicts.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud permits expansion of a subnet's primary IPv4 range after creation if the larger range does not overlap conflicting ranges.

cards.statement: A subnet's secondary IPv4 range can be replaced while instances still use addresses from it.
cards.explanation: A subnet's secondary IPv4 range can be removed or replaced only when no instances use that range.
cards.misconception: Instances can keep using a secondary range while it is replaced.

cards.statement: A reserved static external IP address stays allocated after its VM is deleted.
cards.explanation: A static external IP reservation survives deletion of the VM that used it; release the address resource separately when it is no longer needed.

source.title: Reserve a static external IP address

cards.statement: A reserved static internal IPv4 address can be assigned to a VM in another subnet of the same VPC.
cards.explanation: A static internal IPv4 address belongs to the subnet chosen for its reservation and comes from that subnet's primary range.
cards.misconception: An internal static IP reservation can move between subnets in one VPC.

source.title: Reserve a static internal IP address

cards.statement: A custom static route can name a Compute Engine VM in its VPC network as a next hop.
cards.explanation: A custom static route can name a VM as its next hop when that VM has an interface in the route's VPC network.

cards.statement: Among eligible custom static routes to one destination, a larger priority number takes precedence.
cards.explanation: For eligible custom static routes to the same destination, a smaller priority number has higher priority.
cards.misconception: Larger numeric route priority values win.

cards.statement: A Cloud DNS private zone answers queries from any VPC network in its organization.
cards.explanation: A Cloud DNS private zone answers queries from VPC networks that are authorized for that zone, rather than from the whole organization.
cards.misconception: Private DNS visibility follows organization membership.

cards.statement: gcloud dns record-sets update changes an existing record set in a managed zone.
cards.explanation: The gcloud dns record-sets update command changes a record set within an existing Cloud DNS managed zone.

cards.statement: Public NAT translates outbound traffic from VM internal IPv4 addresses to shared external IPv4 addresses.
cards.explanation: Public NAT gives internet egress to VMs that lack external IPv4 addresses by translating their internal IPv4 traffic through shared external addresses.

cards.statement: One Cloud NAT gateway can serve subnets in several regions of the same VPC network.
cards.explanation: A Cloud NAT gateway is regional and serves configured subnets in that region. Another region needs another gateway.
cards.misconception: One Cloud NAT gateway spans regions.

cards.statement: VPC firewall rules logging records each packet in an allowed TCP connection.
cards.explanation: VPC firewall rules logging records an allowed TCP connection once, rather than recording every packet in that connection.
cards.misconception: Firewall rule logging captures each packet of an allowed connection.

cards.statement: Each Cloud NGFW firewall policy rule has a unique priority within its policy.
cards.explanation: Cloud NGFW requires distinct priority numbers for rules within the same firewall policy, making their evaluation order clear.

cards.statement: Cloud Monitoring can alert when a metric exceeds a configured threshold for a retest window.
cards.explanation: A Cloud Monitoring metric-threshold policy evaluates time-series values against a threshold over its configured retest window.

cards.statement: Cloud Monitoring can write user-defined metric points through the Cloud Logging API.
cards.explanation: User-defined metric points are written through the Cloud Monitoring API, which stores them as time series.
cards.misconception: Cloud Logging API writes custom metric time series.

source.title: Create user-defined metrics with the API

cards.statement: Data Access audit logs are enabled by default for Cloud Storage.
cards.explanation: Data Access audit logs for Cloud Storage need explicit enablement. BigQuery is the default-enabled exception.
cards.misconception: Cloud Storage Data Access logging is on by default.

cards.statement: A Cloud Logging sink can route matching log entries to a BigQuery dataset.
cards.explanation: A Cloud Logging sink filters log entries and can route matches to a write-enabled BigQuery dataset.

cards.statement: Cloud Logging lets you set a custom retention period for a user-defined log bucket.
cards.explanation: User-defined Cloud Logging buckets support a configured retention period that determines how long stored entries remain available.

cards.statement: Cloud Trace groups spans by VM instance rather than by an end-to-end request.
cards.explanation: Cloud Trace groups spans for an end-to-end request under a shared trace ID, so operations across services form one trace.
cards.misconception: A Cloud Trace trace is scoped to one VM.

cards.statement: The Ops Agent collects system metrics and logs from Compute Engine VMs.
cards.explanation: The Ops Agent is the primary telemetry agent for Compute Engine and collects VM system metrics and logs.

cards.statement: Managed collection in Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus scrapes GKE Pods from outside the cluster.
cards.explanation: Managed collection runs Prometheus-based collectors inside the cluster; they scrape local targets and push metrics to Google's datastore.
cards.misconception: Google's central service scrapes GKE Pods remotely.
tags: Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus

cards.statement: Personalized Service Health automatically shows incidents relevant to a selected project.
cards.explanation: Personalized Service Health filters Google Cloud incidents by project relevance and shows affected products and locations.

cards.statement: Active Assist automatically applies recommendations as soon as they appear in the Google Cloud console.
cards.explanation: Active Assist presents recommendations for review; an authorized user applies or dismisses them.
cards.misconception: Active Assist auto-remediates each recommendation when it appears.

cards.statement: Cloud Hub limits its active Google Cloud incident views to individual projects.
cards.explanation: Cloud Hub shows active Google Cloud incidents for a selected project or an App Hub application.
cards.misconception: Cloud Hub cannot display incidents in an application view.
cards.volatilityNote: Cloud Hub's operations views can evolve.

cards.statement: Gemini Cloud Assist investigations can analyze logs, metrics, and configurations during troubleshooting.
cards.explanation: Gemini Cloud Assist investigations use logs, metrics, and configuration context to explore possible root causes.
cards.volatilityNote: Gemini Cloud Assist is a Preview offering with evolving capabilities.

cards.statement: An IAM allow-policy binding associates a principal with a role on a resource.
cards.explanation: An IAM allow policy attaches to a resource and contains role bindings that connect principals to IAM roles.

cards.statement: gcloud projects get-iam-policy displays grants inherited from parent folders.
cards.explanation: gcloud projects get-iam-policy retrieves the policy attached to the project; inherited grants appear in an effective-policy view or the console.
cards.misconception: A project's retrieved policy includes inherited role bindings.

source.title: Manage access to projects, folders, and organizations

cards.statement: An IAM role granted on an organization flows to descendant projects.
cards.explanation: Organization-level IAM role grants apply to descendant folders and projects through allow-policy inheritance.

source.title: Using resource hierarchy for access control

cards.statement: A project admin can remove an inherited IAM role by editing the project's allow policy.
cards.explanation: To edit an inherited IAM grant, change the allow policy on the resource where the role was granted, such as a parent folder.
cards.misconception: A child project's policy can remove a parent grant.

source.title: Manage access to projects, folders, and organizations

cards.statement: IAM basic roles limit permissions to a single Google Cloud service.
cards.explanation: IAM basic roles provide broad permissions across Google Cloud services; service-specific predefined roles are narrower.
cards.misconception: Basic IAM roles are service-scoped.

cards.statement: IAM predefined roles retain the same permission set when Google adds service features.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud manages predefined roles and can update their permissions as services evolve.
cards.misconception: Predefined role permissions remain fixed.

cards.statement: Folders are valid creation scopes for IAM custom roles.
cards.explanation: IAM custom roles are created in an organization or project, not directly in a folder.
cards.misconception: An IAM custom role can be defined on a folder.

cards.statement: A project-level IAM custom role accepts folder administration permissions.
cards.explanation: A project-level IAM custom role cannot include permissions usable only at the folder or organization level.
cards.misconception: Project custom roles can include parent-resource permissions.

cards.statement: An IAM deny policy can block a permission granted by an allow policy.
cards.explanation: IAM evaluates relevant deny policies before allow policies, so a deny rule can override a role grant for a supported permission.

cards.statement: IAM Conditions can limit a role grant using the request time.
cards.explanation: An IAM Condition can evaluate request.time to make a role binding apply during a specified period.

cards.statement: Conditional IAM role bindings use version 3 of the allow-policy schema.
cards.explanation: Version 3 of an IAM allow policy represents conditional role bindings; version 1 omits their conditions.

cards.statement: testIamPermissions checks the caller's permissions on a named resource.
cards.explanation: For supported resources, testIamPermissions returns which requested permissions the authenticated caller has on that resource.

source.title: Test permissions for custom user interfaces

cards.statement: A user-managed service account belongs to a project even when workloads use it elsewhere.
cards.explanation: Each service account is located in one project and cannot be moved to another project after creation.

cards.statement: A project administrator creates and manages service agents used by Google Cloud services.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud creates and manages service agents so its services can access resources on a customer's behalf.
cards.misconception: Project administrators manage service agents like user-managed accounts.

cards.statement: A Compute Engine VM's attached service account supplies credentials to its application.
cards.explanation: Applications on a Compute Engine VM can authenticate to Google Cloud APIs using credentials from the VM's attached service account.

cards.statement: An IAM role granted on a service account controls which resources that account can access.
cards.explanation: Roles granted on a service account resource control who may use or manage that account. Grants to the account on other resources control what it can access.
cards.misconception: The service account's own allow policy controls its outgoing resource access.

cards.statement: The Service Account User role provides the permission to attach a service account to a VM.
cards.explanation: Service Account User includes iam.serviceAccounts.actAs, the permission needed to attach a service account to a VM.

cards.statement: The Service Account Token Creator role lets a principal sign JWTs as a service account.
cards.explanation: Service Account Token Creator includes iam.serviceAccounts.signJwt, which signs JWTs using a Google-managed key.

cards.statement: gcloud impersonation of a service account reads its downloaded private key.
cards.explanation: gcloud impersonation generates short-lived credentials for the target service account instead of using its downloaded key.
cards.misconception: gcloud impersonation requires a target service account key file.

cards.statement: Google rotates user-managed service account keys after they are downloaded.
cards.explanation: Users manage rotation of their user-managed service account keys by replacing old keys and invalidating them.
cards.misconception: Google rotates downloaded service account keys.

source.title: Best practices for managing service account keys

cards.statement: A VM can attach a service account from another project while that project's cross-project usage is disabled.
cards.explanation: Attaching a service account across projects requires disabling the cross-project usage restriction in the service account's project.
cards.misconception: Cross-project service account attachment works under the default restriction.

cards.statement: Workload Identity Federation uses a workload identity pool provider to trust an external IdP.
cards.explanation: A workload identity pool provider defines the trust relationship with an external IdP, allowing external workloads to exchange their credentials for federated access.

cards.statement: Workload Identity Federation for GKE can grant a Kubernetes ServiceAccount direct IAM access to a resource.
cards.explanation: GKE workloads can receive IAM grants as principals representing Kubernetes ServiceAccounts, so direct access does not require an IAM service account.

source.title: About Workload Identity Federation for GKE

cards.statement: GKE Pods using Workload Identity Federation for GKE obtain tokens from the Compute Engine metadata server.
cards.explanation: The GKE metadata server intercepts token requests from Pods using Workload Identity Federation for GKE and returns the credentials.
cards.misconception: GKE Pods still fetch workload tokens from the Compute Engine metadata server.

source.title: About Workload Identity Federation for GKE
